O Beloved, one should visualize her as resembling the rising sun, with the luster of vermilion, two breasts, a bindu at the face, and a throbbing flame of a lamp.
One should meditate upon that [path] from the base (ādhāra) to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by way of the Tantric method:
"O Goddess, Kāma is the Bindu and I am it; the Supreme Goddess resides therein."
O Goddess, below that is the pair of breasts consisting of Śiva and Śakti;
and below that is the supreme digit (kalā) in the form of consciousness, together with the half of a parārdha.
That Kuṇḍalinī energy as well is of the nature of Kāmakalā;
and she too is a threefold creation, consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
The best of practitioners who accomplish through meditation shall bring the three worlds under his control;
even in the absence of a physical consort, he may employ the Great Śakti, the bestower of great siddhis.
Having thus meditated upon oneself in the form of Kāmakalā, and having visualized the Goddess as before,

one should lead the Kuṇḍalinī residing in the Mūlādhāra through the sequence of piercing the six cakras to the Sahasrāra; there, having united her with the Supreme Śiva dwelling therein, and having delighted Him for a mere moment, one should bathe [the deity] with the nectar arising from that union.

Having brought the goddess, who is composed of Brahman and has become one with bliss, from the eight-petaled heart into the path of the breath— like transferring the light from one lamp to another— and having placed her, whose nature is the *bhoja* [the enjoyer], within the handful of flowers representing the *mātṛkās*,
one should establish that flower upon the yantra or other support and, by means of the root mantra, visualize the form of the Goddess.
With palms joined in reverence:
Oṃ! O Goddess of gods, easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by your retinue:
as long as I worship you, remain steadfast here.

Having thus prayed, one should invoke [the deity] with the five mudrās as follows: "O Blessed One, Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā, together with your weapons, together with your vehicle, together with your retinue, accompanied by the illustrious Mahākālabhairava, come here! Stay here! Be present here!"

"Be present here; be manifest here. With palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), perform your empowerment here and accept my worship. Then, holding the *yantra* with the *lelihāna-mudrā*, one should perform the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). As follows: *Āṃ Hrīṃ*.

KROṂ HAṂ SAḤ: The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā are here as vital breaths. Again, ĀṂ HRĪṂ KROṂ HAṂ SAḤ: The life-force (*jīva*) of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā is established here. ĀṂ HRĪṂ KROṂ HAṂ SAḤ: All the sense-faculties (*sarvendriyāṇi*) of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā [are here]. ĀṂ HRĪṂ KROṂ HAṂ SAḤ.

"O Speech, Mind, Sight, Hearing, Smell, and Vital Breath of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā, come here and remain happily for a long time! Svāhā! Then, having recited the Mātṛkā with the Bindu and the Root Mantra over the water of the Arghya offering, one should sprinkle the Goddess and perform the Mahāmudrā of Paramīkaraṇī.

Having displayed [the hand gestures], having veiled [the deity] with the syllable *hūṃ*, having rendered it nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*, having kindled it with the root mantra by means of the *yonimudrā*, and having displayed the *mahāyoni* and *bhūtinī* mudrās, one should perform the ritual adoration after effecting the integration of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the mantras of the six limbs.
The worship consists of the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) as follows:
A seat, a welcome, water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, the honey-mixture, further sipping water, a bath, garments, and ornaments.
One should employ perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and sandalwood as the sixteen articles of worship during the ritual adoration.

The water for the feet, the respectful offering, the water for sipping, likewise the honey-mixture and again water for sipping, and the services beginning with fragrance and ending with the food offering— these are the ten modes of worship in their proper sequence.
One should employ incense, flowers, as well as incense smoke, a lamp, and food offerings in the worship; this constitutes the five-fold ritual service (pañcopacārika) of worship.
First, having uttered the root mantra, one should then state the ritual offering;
one should present that offering in the name of one's own deity.

Therein, first is the worship with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra-pūjā*), as follows: Having brought a seat made of gold or other materials and placed it upon another vessel, one should sprinkle it with the *arghya* water while reciting *phaṭ*, veil it with *hūṃ*, transform it into nectar by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* while reciting *vaṃ*, display the *yoni-mudrā* while reciting the root mantra, and then, having uttered the root mantra, [offer] this:

[Offering] to Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā of such-and-such lineage, obeisance! Then, with palms joined in *añjali*, having recited the root mantra, [say]: "O Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā, welcome! At the end of which, [say] "a very warm welcome.
Then, having recited the root mantra: "This water for the feet (*pādya*) is for Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā, obeisance! Thus [offer] the water.

One should offer [the water] at the feet. Thus: "This is the *arghya*, Śrī [Name], Svāhā. Having combined flowers, *bilva* leaves, *durvā* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), white and red sandalwood, and water into one, one should offer the *arghya* upon the head. "This is the *ācamanīya*, Śrī [Name], Svadhā. Thus, fragrant water is offered in the mouth. This...

"Tailasādhāra-madhuparka, Śrī [0] Svadhā"—thus on the face. "Mūla-mantra: This is the water for sipping again, Śrī [0] Svadhā"—thus on the face. "This is the water for bathing, Śrī [0] Namaḥ"—thus on all limbs. "This is the water for sipping again, as before. "This is the garment, Śrī [0] Namaḥ. "This is the water for sipping again."

"Śrī(0) Svadhā"—thus on the face. "This is the ornament of gold and so forth; Śrī(0) Namaḥ"—thus for the various ornaments. "This is the fragrance; Śrī(0) Namaḥ"—thus on all the limbs. "This is the red unguent; Śrī(0) Namaḥ"—as before. "This is the vermilion; Śrī(0) Namaḥ"—thus one should apply it to the forehead and the parting of the hair.

With the mantra "This flower, Śrī (0) Vauṣaṭ," one should offer various kinds of flowers five times upon the head, heart, secret place, feet, and all limbs. With the mantra "This [offering] with sandalwood and bilva leaves, Śrī (0) Namaḥ," one offers [the flowers] at the two feet. Having offered incense into the fire and consecrated it with sprinkling and other rites, [one offers it with the mantra]: "This incense, Śrī (0)..."

Having offered incense with "Namaḥ," having consecrated the bell with "Phaṭ," and having worshipped the bell with "Oṃ japadhyānamantramātaḥ svāhā" for these perfumes and flowers, one should ring the bell with the left hand while holding the incense aloft with the right hand, moving it up and down as far as the nose.

One should fumigate [the deity] three times. Having lit a lamp with ghee and other substances, and having consecrated it with sprinkling and other rites, one should say, "This is the lamp; obeisance to Śrī," as before, and while ringing the bell, one should show the lamp seven times, raising it high until it reaches the eyes. Then:

Holding the vessel of nectar (*sudhāpātra*) with the left hand in the drinking gesture (*pānamudrā*), and grasping the purification of the ten directions and so forth with the right, one should join the two hands together, placing them against the heart, and recite: *Oṃ mara vaṃ*, [you who are] the Vāruṇī-elixir, the bringer of the end of ten million kalpas.
Accept [this] along with purification; grant me imperishable liberation.

Having recited this and placed the vessel upon the support, one should utter the root mantra: "I offer this pure *āsava*, O Śrī [Name]. Having thus offered it with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), one says:
"Oṃ! To you who are filled with supreme bliss by the delicious taste of the pure *āsava*..."
O Supreme Goddess, protect me in this shoreless cycle of existence.
Then, having drawn a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square facing [the practitioner],
and having placed upon it an offering of various delicious foods together with the vessel for the oblation,
he should worship the food with "Oṃ, salutation to the food-offering (naivedya)," and sprinkle it while reciting "Phaṭ," and [protect it] with "Hūṃ."
Having veiled [the offering] with the syllable *vaṃ* and rendered it nectarine by means of the *dhenumudrā*, having inflamed it with the root mantra (*mūla*) by means of the *yonimudrā*,
having made it complete with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and having covered it with the *matsyamudrā*, one should recite the root mantra ten times therein,
hold it with the left hand using the *tatvamudrā*, and while uttering the root mantra, [offer] this along with its accessories.
"I offer this food offering (naivedya) to the glorious Dakṣiṇakālikā.
Having thus offered it, one should give the water for the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) with: "Oṃ, you are the spreading of the nectar, svāhā. Then: "Oṃ, svāhā to Prāṇa. Oṃ... [etc.]

"Apānāya svāhā! Oṃ samānāya svāhā! Oṃ udānāya svāhā! Oṃ vyānāya svāhā! Having thus displayed the mudrās of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, one says: "Oṃ, I offer this oblation to the Blessed Lady; may she graciously accept it from me. Having thus displayed the *grāsa-mudrā* (the morsel gesture), [one offers] the root mantra and this water for drinking, O Śrī...

I offer this. This root-mantra [is for] the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*); *śrī* [0] *svadhā*. And having consecrated the food offering (*naivedya*) and the betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), I offer this root-mantra [for] the betel leaf; *śrī* [0]. Then, having gratified the Goddess and the Guru three times with the nectar from the *śrīpātra*, one should prostrate. Then, having uttered the root-mantra, this—

"A handful of flowers for the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā, vauṣaṭ! Thus, one should offer five handfuls of flowers upon the head, heart, secret place, feet, and all the limbs. Then, with palms joined in reverence:
"O Great Peace consisting of pure consciousness, O Beloved who delights in the supreme nectar of the sacrificial pap!"
O Kālikā, grant permission for the worship of the retinue.
Having thus obtained permission, one should begin the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
Therein, first is the meditation on the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgadhyāna*):
[the deities] possessing the splendors of frost, crystal, dark-blue, blue, black, and reddish-brown.
The principal female forms hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

Thus, [the mantras] for the head, crest-lock, armor, and eyes of the Goddess are assigned to those [petals]. Alternatively, on an eight-petaled lotus, [one places the syllables] *agnīśa* (Ra) and *sukha* (Ha) upon the filaments; in the center and in the directions starting from the East, [one places]: *cakrāṃ* for the heart, *namaḥ*; *krīṃ* for the head, *svāhā namaḥ*; *krūṃ*.
*Śikhāyai vaṣaṭ namaḥ*. *Kraiṃ kavacāya hūṃ namaḥ*. *Krauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ namaḥ*.

*Kraḥ astrāya phaṭ namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped each limb with sandalwood paste (*gandha*), flowers (*puṣpa*), and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), [one offers] these sandalwood paste and flowers again to the venerable Dakṣiṇakālikā.

"Obeisance to the deities of the six limbs. Having thus worshipped twice, one should satisfy [them] three times with: "Kṛīṃ, I satisfy the deities of the six limbs of the glorious Dakṣiṇakālikā. Then, with the root mantra: "This handful of flowers is for the glorious Dakṣiṇakālikā; Vauṣaṭ!"

Having thus offered a handful of a single flower with the root mantra: *śrīmaddakṣiṇakālikāṃ tarpayāmi svāhā*, one should satisfy the Goddess once and then prostrate. Thereafter, one should worship the venerable Mahākālabhairava.
His mantras are as follows: *oṃ mahākālāya namaḥ*; *hūṃ mahākālāya namaḥ*.

Thus are the two sets of eight syllables: *hūṃ hūṃ mahākāla prasīda prasīda hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā*; *hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ mahākāla hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ*; *oṃ hrīṃ mahākālāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ krīṃ mahākālāya svāhā*. Of these...

For the mantras of Dakṣiṇakālikā: the seer (ṛṣi) is Virāṭ, the meter (chandaḥ) is Sarvavyāpin, the deity (devatā) is the stainless Śrī Mahākālabhairava, the seed-syllable (bīja) is HŪṂ, the power (śakti) is HRĪṂ, the pin (kīlaka) is SVĀHĀ;
the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of the four aims of life—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. [This is recited] at the head.

Salutation to the sage Śrīmaddakṣiṇakālikā. Salutation to the Virāṭ meter in the mouth. Salutation to the all-pervading, stainless deity Śrīmanmahākālabhairava in the heart. Salutation to the seed-syllable *hūṃ* in the secret place. Salutation to the power (*śakti*) *hrīṃ* in the feet. Salutation to the *kīlaka* *svāhā* in all the limbs.

Salutation! The application (viniyoga) is as before. Then, the placement on the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa) is as follows: "Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the lineage of Siddha-gurus beginning with Brahmānandanātha. Having worshipped [the pair] thus twice, one should worship each [individual] separately. These are the scents and flowers: Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ.
Brahmānandanātha Śrīpāda, pūjaya; likewise Pūrṇadevānandanātha Śrīpāda, pūjaya; Calaccittānandanātha Śrīpāda, pūjaya; Calācalānandanātha Śrīpāda, pūjaya;
Kumārānandanātha Śrīpāda, pūjaya; Krodhanānandanātha Śrīpāda, pūjaya.
Having worshipped Varadānandanātha Śrīpāda, Smaradīpanānandanātha Śrīpāda, Māyāmbā Śrīpāda, and Māyāvatyambā Śrīpāda with the nectar from the Guru-vessel, [recite]: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ.

"I offer libations to the gurus of the Siddha lineage, beginning with Brahmānandanātha; salutations. Having thus offered libations three times, one should prostrate; these are the Siddha lineages. Then, with these scents and flowers: "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Vimalānandanātha; salutations. In the same way, [one worships] Kuśalānandanātha.

Śrīpāda Pūjya | Bhīmasenānaṃdanātha Śrīpāda Pūjya | Sudhākarānaṃdanātha Śrīpāda Pūjya | Mīnānaṃdanātha Śrīpāda Pūjya | Gorakṣakānaṃdanātha Śrīpāda Pūjya | Bhogadevānaṃdanātha Śrīpāda Pūjya | Prajāpatyānaṃdanātha Śrīpāda Pūjya.

Pūjā to Mūladevānandanātha Śrīpāda. Pūjā to Raṃtidevānandanātha Śrīpāda. Pūjā to Vighneśvarānandanātha Śrīpāda. Pūjā to Hutāśanānandanātha Śrīpāda. Pūjā to Samayānandanātha Śrīpāda. Pūjā to Saṃtoṣānandanātha Śrīpāda.

Everywhere, one should worship with the mantra ending in "namas," beginning with *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ādiśrīpā... pū...*. With the nectar from the Guru-vessel, one should offer libations three times, saying: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ vimalānandanāthādi-manavaugha-gurūṃs tarpayāmi namaḥ*, and then prostrate. Thereafter, [the ritual of] Kālī and so forth...
One should worship the fifteen Nityās by proceeding counter-clockwise from the letters of the inner triangle. Her visualization (dhyāna) is as follows:

All [the goddesses] are dark-complexioned, holding swords in their hands, adorned with garlands of severed heads, holding a threatening gesture (tarjanī) with their left hands, possessing pure smiles, naked, and with laughing faces.

Having meditated thus: "Accompanied by their respective husbands," [one offers] this *pādya* (water for the feet): *krīṃ*, obeisance to the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Kālī. Having worshipped in this sequence with offerings ending in food (*naivedya*) and betel (*tāmbūla*), one worships again:
these perfumes and flowers, *krīṃ*, obeisance to Kālī; likewise to Kapālinī and Kullā.

In the outer triangle there, [worship] Kuru, Kullā, Virodhinī, and Vipracittā; in the outer triangle beyond that, Ugraprabhā and Dīptā; in the outer triangle beyond that, Nīlā, Ghanā, and Valākā; in the outer triangle beyond that, Mātṛkā, Mudrā, and Mitā. These [names] should be preceded by the seed-syllable *krīṃ* and ended with *namaḥ*.

One should worship. Thus, the authoritative measurement has been stated in the Rudrayāmala: "The powers beginning with Kālī should be worshipped solely by means of the seed-syllable of Kālī; otherwise, there would be a loss of accomplishment in the supreme worship of Kālikā.
Then, having offered libations three times with: *krīṃ, I offer libations to the fifteen powers beginning with Kālī, svāhā*.
One should prostrate.

Then, having recited the root mantra, one should offer a handful of flowers with the words: "This handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) is offered with vauṣaṭ to the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā, who resides upon the seat of the three pentads (tripañcāra-pīṭha) together with the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Kālī. Having thus offered the handful of flowers, [one should continue].
One should satisfy [the deities] once. Then, on the eight petals, one should worship the eight Śaktis beginning with Brāhmī by moving counter-clockwise.

Therein, first, having worshipped with everything from "This is the water for the feet: Hrīṃ, obeisance to the eight Śaktis beginning with Brāhmī" up to the offerings of food and betel, [one should offer] again: "These are the perfume and flowers: Hrīṃ."
"Salutation to the eight powers beginning with Brahmā. Having thus worshipped [the group], one should worship each individually, starting from the east:
"Oṃ, salutation to Brāhmī; likewise, Īṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇī;
Jaṃ, salutation to Māheśvarī; Ṛṃ, salutation to Cāmuṇḍā; Ḷṃ, salutation to Kaumārī; Aiṃ..."
"Salutation to Aparājitā; Oṃ, salutation to Vārāhī; Aṃḥ, salutation to Nārasiṃhī.
Having thus worshipped, one should offer libations three times with: "Hrīṃ, I offer libations to the eight Śaktis beginning with Brahmā;
salutation. Then, having recited the root mantra, one should present this handful of flowers upon the petals of the eight-petaled lotus.

"To Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā, together with the eight powers beginning with Brahmā, Vauṣaṭ. Having thus offered a handful of flowers, one should recite the root mantra and offer libations once, saying: "I satisfy Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā, Svāhā. Then, at the tips of the eight petals, [one offers] this water for the feet: "Oṃ, obeisance to the eight Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga."

Having thus worshipped with offerings ending with the food offering (*naivedya*) and betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), one should worship again with these perfumes and flowers, saying once: "Oṃ, salutation to the eight Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga. Then, one should worship each individually, starting from the east and proceeding counter-clockwise (*vāmāvartena*): "Aṃ, salutation to Asitāṅgabhairava; Iṃ, salutation to Rurubhairava."

Ṭhaṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍabhairava; Ṛṃ, obeisance to Krodhabhairava; Ḷṃ, obeisance to Unmattabhairava; Eṃ, obeisance to Kapālībhairava; Oṃ, obeisance to Bhīṣaṇabhairava; Aṃ, obeisance to Saṃhārabhairava. Having thus worshipped with perfumes and flowers: Oṃ.
"I offer libations to the eight Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga; obeisance. Having thus offered libations three times, one should prostrate.

Then, having recited the root mantra: "This handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) is for the venerable Dakṣiṇakālikā, together with the eight Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga, at the tips of the eight petals; vauṣaṭ. Having thus offered the handful of flowers, one should recite the root mantra.

"I satisfy the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā, svāhā! Having thus offered libations once, one should prostrate. Outside of that, in the region of the *bhūpura*, one should worship the ten guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra, in a clockwise direction starting from the east. "This is the water for the feet; Oṃ, obeisance to the ten guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra. Thus [one should offer].

Having worshipped as before, [offering] these perfumes and flowers with "Oṃ, obeisance to the ten guardians of the directions beginning with Indra," one should worship each of them individually with these perfumes and flowers: "Laṃ, obeisance to Indra; Raṃ, obeisance to Agni."
Maṃ, obeisance to Yama; kṣaṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti; vaṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa; yaṃ, obeisance to Vāyu;
kuṃ, obeisance to Kubera; huṃ, obeisance to Īśāna; between the East and Īśāna, āṃ, obeisance to Brahmā; between Nirṛti and Varuṇa, hrīṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Thus.
Having performed the worship: "Oṃ, I satiate Indra and the other guardians of the ten directions. Having thus satiated them three times, one should prostrate.

Then, having recited the root mantra: "This handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) is for the venerable Dakṣiṇakālikā together with Indra and the other guardians of the ten directions; vauṣaṭ. Having thus offered the handful of flowers, one should recite the root mantra.

"I offer libations to the glorious Dakṣiṇakālikā, svāhā! Having thus offered the libations, one should prostrate. Then, outside the outer square (bhūpura), one should worship as before with "Oṃ, obeisance to the weapons beginning with the Vajra," and so forth, saying: "These are the perfume and flowers; Oṃ, obeisance to the weapons beginning with the Vajra. Then, for each [item] individually...

One should worship with perfumes and flowers. With these perfumes and flowers: *vaṃ* homage to Vajra; likewise, *śaṃ* homage to Śakti; *iṃ* homage to Daṇḍa; *khaṃ* homage to Khaḍga; *pāṃ* homage to Pāśa; *aṃ* homage to Aṅkuśa; *oṃ gaṃ* homage to Gadā; *śūṃ* homage to Śūla.

Between the east and the northeast: *paṃ* to the lotus, *namaḥ*. Between the southwest (*nirṛti*) and the west (*varuṇa*): *caṃ* to the discus, *namaḥ*. Then, having offered libations three times with the mantra: *oṃ vajrāṅgādy-astrāṇi tarpayāmi*, one should prostrate. Then, as before, having offered a handful of flowers to the Goddess and offered libations, one should prostrate. Then...

One should worship the weapons of the Goddess. In her lower left hand are these: *gaṃ* for scent and *puṣpe* for flowers. "Muṃ, obeisance to Muṇḍa," thus three times. "Muṃ, I satiate Muṇḍa," thus three times. Likewise, in her upper left hand: "Khaṃ, obeisance to Khaḍga," and "Khaṃ, I satiate Khaḍga," thus three times. In her hand above that, *aṃ*.

"Obeisance to Abhayā (the Fearless One). "Aṃ, I satiate Abhayā. Thus three times. Then one should worship the Goddess, together with her weapons and her retinue, with the five services beginning with perfume (gandha). [Recite] the root mantra: "This perfume, obeisance to the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā, together with her weapons and her vehicle. In this same manner...

Having worshipped [her] with betel leaves and other offerings in due order, offer three handfuls of flowers while reciting: "This is the offering of sandalwood and flowers (puṣpāñjali) to the venerable Dakṣiṇakālī, together with her weapons, her vehicle, her retinue, and accompanied by the illustrious Mahākālabhairava; vauṣaṭ. Having thus offered the three handfuls of flowers, recite the root mantra.
"I offer libations to the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālī, together with her weapons, her vehicle, and her retinue, accompanied by the illustrious Mahākālabhairava; svāhā!
Having thus offered libations three times, one should prostrate. One should present the sacrificial offering (bali). On the ground before the Goddess, [one should draw] a triangle within a circle...

Having fashioned a square mandala and arranged an offering (bali) of liquor, meat, cooked rice, and so forth, one should hold it with the left hand using the *tatvamudrā* and, grasping the vessel of the offering with the right hand, recite: "Kṛṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, svāhā to the glorious Dakṣiṇakālikā! This is the offering; obeisance! Thus, one should present the offering with the food offerings (*naivedya*) and other items.
"One should give"—this is the *sāttvika* offering. Now, as for the *rājasa* offering:
having bathed an animal such as a goat possessing auspicious marks and having placed it before the Goddess, [one should proceed].

Having recited the root mantra and looked [at the object], one should sprinkle it with the *argha* water while saying *phaṭ*; strike it with *kuśa* grass while saying *phaṭ*; and veil it while saying *hūṃ*. Then, into the right ear, one should recite three times: "Oṃ, may we know Paśu-pāśa; may we meditate upon Viśvakarman; may Jīva impel us. [This is repeated] into the left ear.
Once, he should cause the animal to hear the *gāyatrī* mantra. Then [he offers]: "This is water for the feet; *oṃ*, salutation to the goat-animal (*chāgapaśu*).

Likewise, this is the respectful offering (*arghya*), this is water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), this is the fragrance, these are the sandalwood and flowers, this is the incense, this is the lamp, this is the food offering (*naivedya*) with its accessories, this is water for drinking, and this is water for sipping."

"This is the betel-roll. Having thus worshipped, one should worship the sword [with]: "This is the water for the feet; *hūṃ*, obeisance to the sword," and so forth, up to the offerings of food (*naivedya*) and betel-roll. Then, at the tip of the sword: "These are the sandalwood paste and flowers; *oṃ*..."

Salutation to Vāgīśvarī and Brahmā. Likewise in the middle of the sword: Oṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. At the base of the sword: Oṃ, salutation to Umā and Maheśvara. Then: Oṃ, [salutation] to Him who is joined with the powers of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.

"Salutation to Khaḍga. Having thus worshipped, one should prostrate with this mantra: "Oṃ, salutation to you, O Lord Khaḍga, the destroyer of enemies, intent upon the task of power, the swift sword for the severing of the bonds of the bound soul (paśu).
Then, taking a vessel made of copper or another material, and placing within it sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and water, one should hold it with the right hand while [supporting it] with the left hand.

Having seized the sacrificial animal: *Oṃ*. Today, in the month of [name], when the sun is in the zodiac sign of [name], in the fortnight of [name], on the lunar day of [name], [I], of the [name] lineage, the venerable [name] Śarmā, for the pleasure of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā, offer this goat or sheep as a sacrificial animal with Agni as its presiding deity, or this deer as a sacrificial animal with Vāyu as its presiding deity.

"I shall cause the buffalo animal, whose presiding deity is Yama, to be sacrificed for you, O Blessed One, Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā; I shall cause it to be sacrificed for the sake of others"—this is the distinction. Having thus made the resolve, with palms joined in *añjali*, one should recite: "Oṃ, according to the prescribed rite, may this be offered unto you. Then:

Raising the sword, one should apply it to the shoulder of the sacrificial animal with the mantra: *oṃ chindi chindi hūṃ phaṭ*. Then, having positioned the animal facing east and tied it to a pillar or similar support, the cutter, facing north, [should invoke] the Goddess.

Intent on meditation, one should cut [the head] with a single stroke. Then, having placed the flesh and blood into a skull-cup or similar vessel, one should recite the root mantra: "This offering of flesh and blood, I bestow upon you, O Blessed Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā. Having thus offered it, [one places it] upon the severed head.

Having prepared a lamp with a wick soaked in ghee and reciting the root mantra, one should offer it, saying: "This goat-head offering accompanied by a lamp, I bestow upon you, O venerable Dakṣiṇakālikā. Then, having divided the blood fallen on the ground into five portions, [one should offer them] starting from the east and proceeding clockwise as previously described.

Having offered the *bali* to the *baṭukas*, *yoginīs*, *kṣetrapālas*, and *gaṇeśas* with their respective *mantras*, one should offer the *bali* to all beings (*sarvabhūtas*) in the center. This is the procedure for the offering of the *bali*.
Then, having performed *prāṇāyāma* and having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times or one thousand times—
or if unable, thirty-eight times— having again performed *prāṇāyāma* and so forth,

and taking water with flowers for the *arghya* offering, [one should contemplate] the fruit of the recitation in the form of light by means of the mantra beginning with "guhyātiguhyagoptā... and so on.

Having offered [the water] into the left hand of the Goddess, one should recite "Oṃ Mūlaṃ Oṃ" seven times for the removal of impurity (*aśaucabhaṅga*) and prostrate. I shall describe the procedure for the special recitation (*viśeṣajapa*) below. If one is capable, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*), as follows:
in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or on level ground, measuring one span (*prādeśa*)...

Having drawn three lines with their tips pointing eastward, having gazed upon them with the root mantra, having sprinkled them with the water for the *arghya* offering while reciting "Phaṭ," having struck them with *kuśa* grass while reciting "Phaṭ," and having sprinkled them while reciting "Huṃ," one should worship them with: "Obeisance to these perfumes and flowers on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā. Then, having brought the fire:

Having consecrated it as before with the gazing and other rites, one should cast out the portion for the flesh-eaters (kravyāda) toward the southwest with the mantra: "HŪṂ PHAṬ, obeisance to the flesh-eaters, SVĀHĀ," using a single glowing piece of wood placed there. Then, having established the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) containing the fire facing oneself, [one recites] HRĪṂ.

"Salutation to the form of Fire (Vahnimūrtaye namaḥ). Salutation to the consciousness of Fire (Raṃ Vahnicaitanyāya namaḥ). Having thus worshipped and having conceptualized the form and consciousness of the Fire, one should kindle the fire with the Jvālinī-mudrā while reciting: "Oṃ Cit-piṅgala, slay, slay! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Churn, churn! Command all, cause to know! Svāhā!"
Oṃ, I pay homage to Agni, the blazing one, the knower of all beings, the consumer of oblations—
pure, golden-hued, kindled, and facing in every direction.

Having thus prostrated before the fire with palms joined in reverence, he assigns the name to the fire, saying: "Oṃ, Agni, you are named Śrīmad-Dakṣiṇakālikā. Then, having given the fire its name, he says: "O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, come here; O Lohitākṣa, accomplish all rites, svāhā! To this fire named Śrīmad-Dakṣiṇakālikā, salutations with these perfumes and flowers."

Having worshipped [the deity] with these and other [mantras], one should take clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Having inspected it with the root mantra, sprinkled it with *phaṭ*, struck it with *kuśa* grass while reciting *phaṭ*, and sprinkled it while reciting *hūṃ*, one should place two *kuśa* blades—one as long as a span (*prādeśa*) and the other white and red in form—into it. Then, having divided the clarified butter into three parts, [place them] on the left.
Having meditated on the *iḍā* in the right [nostril], the *piṅgalā* in the left, and the *suṣumnā* in the middle, one says "namaḥ.

Then, taking clarified butter from the right side, one should offer it into the right eye of the fire with "oṃ agnaye svāhā" and say "namaḥ. Then, taking clarified butter from the left side, one offers it into the left eye of the fire with "oṃ somāya svāhā" and says "namaḥ."

Having thus taken clarified butter from the middle portion, [one says]: "Oṃ agniṣomābhyāṃ svāhā. [One applies it] on the forehead and the eyes with "punarnamaḥ. Having then taken clarified butter from the right side, one should offer it into his mouth with "Oṃ agnaye sviṣṭikṛte svāhā. Thereafter, one should perform the Mahāvyāhṛti homa.

One should offer oblations three times, saying: *oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ svaḥ svāhā*, and *oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā*. Then, having meditated upon the Goddess in the fire and invoked Her, one should worship Her with the five offerings beginning with fragrance (*gandha*) and perform the oblation of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-huti*): *oṃ krāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ svāhā*; *oṃ krīṃ*... [etc.]
*Śirase svāhā*. *Oṃ krūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ svāhā*. *Oṃ kraiṃ kavacāya huṃ svāhā*.
*Oṃ krauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ svāhā*. *Oṃ kraḥ astrāya phaṭ*. Then, having recited the Mahākāla mantra: *Śrīmanmahākālabhairavāya svāhā*, one should offer oblations three times.
One should offer oblations to the eight Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga: *aṃ* to Asitāṅgabhairava, svāhā;
*iṃ* to Rurubhairava, svāhā; *uṃ* to Caṇḍabhairava, svāhā; *ṛṃ* to Krodhabhairava, svāhā; *ḷṃ* to Unmattabhairava, svāhā; *eṃ* to Kapālībhairava, svāhā; *oṃ*... [to Bhīṣaṇabhairava, svāhā].
Svāhā to Bhīṣaṇabhairava! Svāhā to Aṃ Saṃhārabhairava! Then, having recited the root mantra: Svāhā to the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā! Thus is the sixteen-fold oblation.
Having offered either twenty-five oblations or [the full set], one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). With the *sruva* ladle, that clarified butter—
Having taken hold [of the water] and recited the root mantra: "From this time forward, by virtue of my life-force, intellect, body, and authority over dharma,
in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, through mind, speech, and action, and with both hands..."

Whatever has been done by my feet, my belly, or my genitals; whatever has been remembered, spoken, or performed—may all that be an offering unto Brahman. I offer myself and everything belonging to me at the feet of the supreme deity, the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālī. Svāhā! Oṃ tat sat. Then:

Having brought the Goddess from the presence of the fire back to one's own heart by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should dismiss the fire with the words, "O Fire, forgive me. Then, having cooled [the vessel] with curd or water, saying, "O Earth, be cool," one should apply a tilaka mark on the forehead with the ashes clinging to the *sruva* ladle, using the mantra beginning with "Oṃ Yaṃ... and so forth. Thus.
The rule for the daily fire-oblation.
Thereafter, one should recite the root mantra with particular care.
Now, the procedure for recitation is as follows:

if one recites at a time other than during the period of worship, then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and the expulsion of obstructive spirits (*bhūtāpasāraṇa*), [one should take] the seat.

Having purified [the area], one should sit there. Then, having prostrated to the four Gurus above the left ear, to Gaṇeśa on the right, and to one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevī) in the center, and having performed the breath control (prāṇāyāma), the assignment of seers (ṛṣyādi), and the ritual placements on the limbs (aṅganyāsa),
one should contemplate the crest of the mantra (maṃtraśikhā) with the mantra *haṃ saḥ*.

Having sequentially joined [the breath] from the *mūlādhāra* and the other six *cakras* up to the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus situated at the head, one should unite it with the Supreme Śiva; having delighted there for even a moment, [one should remain].

Having bathed [the mantra] in the nectar arising from that, one should bring it back to the *mūlādhāra*. Having performed this in sequence seven times, the radiance (*tejas*) that arises is the *mantra-śikhā*. Then, one should contemplate the consciousness (*caitanya*) of the mantra.
As before, having united the *kuṇḍalinī* with the Supreme Śiva in the *sahasrāra* and having delighted [Him] with her, [one should proceed].

Having bathed [the deity] with the nectar arising therefrom, and having brought it back to the *mūlādhāra*, one should contemplate the two seed-syllables *haṃ haṃ* within the *suṣumnā*, which consists of the forms of the moon, sun, and fire; then,

having meditated upon the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) enveloped therein as being of the nature of light, [one should place it] again in the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*), within the triangular mandala beginning with *a*, *ka*, and *tha*.
Having visualized the root mantra encapsulated by those two seed-syllables, one should bathe it with lunar nectar (*candrāmṛta*).

Thus is the consciousness of the mantra (*mantracaitanya*); thereafter, one should contemplate the meaning of the mantra. The meaning of the mantra is as follows: one should visualize the beloved Goddess, whose nature is the mantra, within the six cakras beginning with the *mūlādhāra*, as well as in the *sahasrāra*. Then—

Having meditated upon the venerable Guru in the thousand-petaled lotus, one should worship him with mental offerings. Having meditated upon the chosen Goddess in the heart, one should worship her with mental offerings. One should recite the *kullukā* mantra—*krīṃ hūṃ strīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ*—ten times over the head. One should recite the *setu* mantra—*aiṃ hūṃ aiṃ*—ten times in the heart.

One should recite "Kṛīṃ," the Great Embankment (*mahāsetu*), ten times at the throat. One should recite "Aiṃ" [followed by] the Root Mantra [and] "Aiṃ," the Removal of Curses (*śāpoddhāra*), ten times. One should recite the Ajā-mantra—"Klīṃ Aiṃ Aiṃ Blūṃ Blūṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hūṃ Oṃ Strīṃ Svāhā"—ten times. Then, one should recite "Nirvāṇa" ten times and once at the navel.
As follows: Oṃ aṃ mūlaṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aṃḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ.
ña ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ta tha da dha na pa pha ba bha ma ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha la kṣa | oṃ mūlam | oṃ kṣaṃ laṃ haṃ saṃ ṣaṃ saṃ vaṃ laṃ raṃ yaṃ maṃ bhaṃ baṃ ||
phaṃ paṃ naṃ dhaṃ daṃ thaṃ taṃ ṇaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭaṃ ñaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ chaṃ caṃ ñaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ khaṃ kaṃ aṃḥ aṃ auṃ oṃ aiṃ eṃ ḹṃ ḷṃ ṝṃ ṛṃ ūṃ uṃ āṃ aṃ mūlam.

Oṃ. Then, at the base of the *liṅga*, one should recite "krīṃ" ten times on the head and the forehead. Then, one should meditate upon the deity as being of the very nature of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), from the head down to the feet of the deity; this is the secret convention (*saṃketa*) of the mantra. Next is the knowledge of the constituent parts of the mantra.
He who performs the recitation of mantras while the senses, such as hearing and the rest, are inactive,
shall encounter poverty, misfortune, and even the attainment of hell.
They know the *bindu* to be the ear, the *nāda* the mouth, and the letter *ka* the heart; the fire-eye (*vahni-netra*) is the *kīlaka*. One should speak of the beloved for a long duration of time.
Regarding the visualization of the locations of mantras:
Mantras that abide in their proper locations grant boons, and those established in the visualization of the mantra also bestow boons;
however, those devoid of both location and visualization are enemies, even if they are pure.
In this context, O fair-faced one, I shall describe that locus:
the Sakala, the Niṣphala, the Sūkṣma, and likewise the Sakalaniṣphala.
Established in the *bindu*, it is differentiated by the *kalās*; above that is what transcends the *kalās*.
That indeed is the *Kulakuṇḍalinī*, declared by Śiva as the power of *nāda*.
Those who remain in this place are proclaimed as "abiding in the place" (sthānastha) when reciting the mantra. As for meditation,
it consists of the secret convention of the mantra as well as the contemplation of its constituent parts.
O Īśānī, that mantra-meditation was previously taught by Śambhu.

Then the *jhillirā* should recite the encapsulated mantra ten times or once, as follows: *haṃ śrīṃ klīṃ oṃ klīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ strīṃ strīṃ svāhā mūlaṃ svāhā | strīṃ strīṃ hūṃ hūṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*.

*Klīṃ oṃ eṃ klīṃ śrīṃ haṃ*. Then, at the beginning and end of the recitation, one should recite the root mantra encapsulated by the *bhūtalipi* three times each, as follows: *aṃ iṃ uṃ ṛṃ ḷṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ haṃ yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ ṅaṃ kaṃ khaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ ñaṃ caṃ chaṃ jhaṃ*.
jaṃ ṇaṃ ṭaṃ ḍhaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ naṃ taṃ thaṃ dhaṃ daṃ maṃ paṃ phaṃ bhaṃ baṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ mūlaṃ saṃ ṣaṃ śaṃ vaṃ bhaṃ phaṃ paṃ maṃ daṃ dhaṃ thaṃ taṃ naṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ chaṃ ñaṃ gaṃ.
Ghaṃ khaṃ kaṃ ṅaṃ laṃ vaṃ raṃ yaṃ haṃ auṃ oṃ aiṃ eṃ ḷṃ ṛṃ uṃ iṃ aṃ— this is the *bhūtalipi*.
Then one should recite the mantra of the Ḍākinīs and others ten times or once, as follows:

Ḍāṃ ḍiṃ ḍamaravarayīṃ, O Ḍākinī, you whose nature is Durgā, protect me, protect me! Root mantra: *namaḥ* to Ḍākinī. Rāṃ rīṃ ramaravarayīṃ, O Rākinī, you whose nature is Durgā, protect me, protect me! Root mantra: *namaḥ* to Rākinī. Lāṃ līṃ lamaravarayīṃ, O Lākinī... [protect me, protect me! Root mantra: *namaḥ* to Lākinī.

Protect, protect me, O Durgātmikā! Root mantra: *Lākinyai namaḥ*. *Kāṃ Kīṃ Kamaravarayīṃ*, O Kākinī, protect me, protect me, O Durgātmikā! Root mantra: *Kākinyai namaḥ*. *Śāṃ Śīṃ Śamaravarayīṃ*, O Śākinī, protect me, protect me, O Durgātmikā! Root mantra: *Śākinyai namaḥ*.
Hāṃ hīṃ hamaravarayīṃ hākinī, protect me, protect me, O Durgātmikā! Homage to the root-mantra for Rākini.
Then, the purification of the mouth: Krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ oṃ krīṃ kriṃ krīṃ—[recite this] ten times in the mouth.
One should recite [the mantra]. Then, one should recite the *caura* mantra ten times at each door, or once at each:

*krauṃ* at the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), *hrīṃ hrīṃ* on the two eyes, *hrīṃ hrīṃ* on the two ears, *huṃ huṃ* on the mouth, *śrīṃ śrīṃ* at the navel, *hsauḥ hsauḥ* at the *liṅga*, and *klīṃ klīṃ*.
At the secret place, *blūṃ blūṃ*; between the eyebrows, *hūṃ phaṭ*. Then, one should contemplate the unity of the Guru, the mantra, and the deity in the form of light within the heart.
Thereafter, one should visualize the *yonimudrā* as follows:
Having visualized the three-yoni at the crown of the head, one should remember the great yoni in the heart;
the nine-cornered [yoni] at the base of the navel, and the triangle at the *mūlādhāra*.

The foremost of practitioners should meditate upon the power of the *liṅga* in the thousand-petaled lotus; O Dear One, [he should meditate] upon the womb of desire (*kāmayoni*) in the root-lotus, resembling ten million flashes of lightning.
One should remember the swan-source at the base of the navel, the knowledge-source in the heart,
the world-source in the thousand-spoked [lotus], and one should constantly remember the seed of the source.

If one is capable of meditating on the *yonimudrā*, one should recite the root mantra ten times enclosed by the *yonibīja* "hlāṃ" and "hlīṃ," as follows: "hlāṃ [root mantra] hlīṃ. Then, having uttered the mantra "oṃ śrīṃ oṃ hūṃ oṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ," one should purify the tongue with water. Hrīṃ.

One should recite the root mantra *hrīṃ* seven times for the union of the vital breath (*prāṇayoga*). One should recite the illuminator (*dīpanī*) *klīṃ*—the root mantra *klīṃ*—seven times. One should recite the dispeller of sleep (*nidrābhaṅga*) *iṃ*—the root mantra *iṃ*—seven times. One should recite the dispeller of grief (*aśocabhaṅga*) *oṃ*—the root mantra *oṃ*—seven times. This is the principle of the individual soul (*jīvatattva*).

One should recite "aṃ kaṃ caṃ ṭaṃ taṃ paṃ yaṃ śaṃ mūlaṃ śaṃ yaṃ paṃ taṃ ṭaṃ caṃ kaṃ aṃ" ten times or three times. Then one should perform the recitation using a rosary of letters, or a secret rosary made of human teeth and so forth, or a crystal rosary, or a finger-counting rosary (karamālā). [The following is] the purification of the finger-counting rosary:
For example: *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ karamāle phaṭ svāhā*.

Having recited this once on each joint (*parvan*) and once on the *meru* bead, one should purify it by reciting *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ strīṃ* once on each joint and once on the *meru*, as before. This applies to rosaries made of crystal and other such materials.
Hrīṃ! O Mālā, O Mālā, O Great Mālā, whose nature is all-pervading power!
Since the fourfold aims of human life are entrusted to you, therefore, be the bestower of success upon me.

Having bathed [the rosary] three times with the supreme nectar (paramāmṛta) using the mantra "iti," and having worshipped it with offerings beginning with water for the feet (pādya) and ending with food (naivedya) and betel (tāmbūla), saying: "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Akṣamālikā; this is the water for the feet," one should then satisfy it three times, saying: "Hrīṃ, I satisfy Akṣamālikā, Svāhā," and prostrate.
Hrīṃ! O Mālā, always ensure that there is no obstacle for me at the time of my recitation;
O Goddess of gods, O Akṣamālā, grant me freedom from obstacles; salutations to you.
The specific mantra for the great garland of conch shells is as follows:
HŪṂ HRĪṂ HŪṂ OṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ OṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ HUṂ OṂ SVĀHĀ | OṂ HŪṂ MAHĀYOGINI TRIBHUVANATĀRIṆI MAHĀŚAṄKHĀSTHI MADHYE NIVĀSAṂ KURU KURU ||

Bestow, bestow all accomplishments! Accept, accept the offerings of wine and meat! *hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!* This offering of wine and meat, this *bali* sacrifice, is for the Great Conch-Eyed One (*mahāśaṅkhākṣa*) and the Rosary (*mālikā*); obeisance! All [the rest] is as before, without exception. Thus.
Having prostrated and meditated upon the oneness of the Guru, the Mantra, and the Deity as being of the nature of radiant light,
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, or a thousand, or ten thousand; then, placing the rosary upon the head with palms joined in reverence:
Hrīṃ! O Garland, you are considered the bestower of delight and auspiciousness to all the gods;
grant me welfare, O Blessed One, and bestow upon me fame and valor.

Having thus offered praise, performed the *prāṇāyāma* and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other elements, and having recited the *kullukā* ten times on the head, the *setu* ten times at the heart, and the *mahāsetu* ten times at the throat, one should then recite the root mantra three times with the *dhūti-īṣyā-puṭa* [breathing technique], and place the water of the *argha* offering along with flowers in the right hand.
O Protectress of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us;
O Great Goddess, may accomplishment be mine through your grace.
Having offered the fruit of the recitation (japa), in the form of radiant energy, into the left hand of the Goddess with this mantra,
and having recited "Oṃ Mūla Oṃ" seven times to break the impurity, and having recited the previously mentioned *jīvatattva* three times,
one should lift [the deity] from the head and prostrate.
You are Kālikā, the Night of Time; you are the bestower of boons upon the three worlds; you alone have become the perfected being (Siddhi).
You are the single Śakti who is divided into three forms, the supreme one who is beyond the control of others, she whose form is the Great Haṃsa.
[You are] desire, the pillar, earth, water, fire, wind, and the principle of space.

May Ugratārā protect me— she who dwells within the belly of all, the mother of the three worlds, whose nature is that of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, who exists in the form of Kuṇḍalī, and who resides in both Kula and Akula.
Another mantra for prostration is found in the *Tantraratna*:
"O Mother Hari, who consists of compassion, who fulfills all hopes, O Goddess Kālikā, giver of boons and enjoyments, salutations to you."
Having prostrated with this [verse], or else one should prostrate three times with the verse beginning "O you who are the auspiciousness of all" (*sarvamaṅgala*).
One should also prostrate three times to the Guru with the verses beginning "The unbroken circle" (*akhaṇḍamaṇḍala*). He now states the definition of the three types of prostration and so forth.
Salutation is mental, divine, physical, and likewise vocal;
among these three types of homage, the physical is considered the most excellent.
A single prostration with one hand, or even a single circumambulation,
and the sight of Viṣṇu at an improper time— this is the merit previously performed.
In another tantra it is said:
"Salutation is traditionally held by the knowers of reality to be threefold—bodily, vocal, and mental; among these, the bodily is considered the highest, while the vocal is the middle."
When performed by men using either Puranic or Vedic mantras,
that vocal salutation (vācika-namaskāra) shall always be considered middling.
When a salutation is performed by one endowed with devotion, composed personally in both prose and verse,
it is remembered as the highest form of vocal [worship].
Having gone to the ground on one's knees and touched the earth with the head,
the salutation that is performed is known as the supreme physical prostration.
Having folded the hands like a *puṭī* and placed them upon the head in that manner,
without touching the ground with the knees and shanks, it is called *sodham*.
The five-limbed prostration is as follows:
"With both arms, with both knees, with the head, with speech, and with the intellect—
the wise have proclaimed this as the five-limbed prostration."
The eight-limbed prostration is as follows:
With the two arms, the two feet, the body, the chest, the head, the eyes,
the mind, and the speech— this is declared to be the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
In the longing for the power of Hari,
one who has fallen to the ground even once should not cease prostrating repeatedly;
rising again and again, one should perform prostrations like a staff.
Elsewhere as well:
One should not perform recitation, fire-offerings, or prostrations in front of, behind, to the left of, near, or inside the inner sanctum of a temple.
Regarding Vārāhī:

"That man who bows to me while his body is covered by a garment shall be born as a leper and a fool for seven future births. Regarding circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*), it is as stated in the Kālikāpurāṇa:
Extending his right hand while bowing his body himself,
he should again show his right side, being right-minded even in thought.
One should properly wrap it three times clockwise around Kālikā;
that clockwise wrapping is to be known as the bestower of satisfaction upon the entire host of gods.
In the *Mantradarpaṇa*:
"Holding the arghya vessel in his hand and ringing the bell with his left, the practitioner of mantra should perform circumambulation; this rule is prescribed for all instances."
And in the *Rahasya*:
"He who performs one hundred and eight circumambulations of Kālikā attains all desires and thereafter shall attain liberation."
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"He who performs three circumambulations of the Prasāda thereafter obtains,
at every step, the fruit of the horse sacrifice."
In the *Tārārahasyavṛtti*:
"By giving land to those who know the Vedas, one obtains that fruit which is the fruit of a perfectly performed sacrifice;
by performing a circumambulation even once, one attains that same fruit."
"One should perform one circumambulation for Caṇḍī, seven for the Sun, three for Vināyaka,
four for Keśava, and half a circumambulation for Śiva."
He states the proper place for prostration in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "If [the prostration] is toward the east, one meets death; if toward the back, it is said to cause decline;
if on the left side, there will be destruction; but on the right, it grants all desires."
Thus, having recited the hymns, armor-mantras (*kavaca*), and so forth, and having offered three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the Goddess as before;
having bowed again, lit the incense and lamps, and presented them to the Goddess, one should perform the *ārārtika* ceremony.
As follows: preceded by the sounding of the bell and other instruments, having perfumed [the deity] with incense and raised the lamp, [beginning from the feet...]

Having displayed it ten times up to the head, one should rotate it three times above the head. Having offered water three times, one should wipe it with a moist cloth. Then, having bowed again, lifted the special *arghya*, and offered the *saṃhāra-arghya*, one should take the *ciluka* water.
One should perform the surrender of the self as follows:

"Whatever has been done by me from this point forward—through the authority of my life-force, intellect, body, and duties; in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; with a well-disposed mind, through speech, and through action;
by means of the two hands, the feet, the abdomen, and the genitals; whatever has been remembered, whatever has been spoken..."

"Whatever has been done, may all that be an offering to Brahman; I offer myself and everything belonging to me at the feet of the Supreme Deity, the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā—svāhā! Having thus offered [the oblation] with the root mantra "Oṃ Tat Sat," one should stand with palms joined in reverence.
O Śivā, whether done knowingly or unknowingly, whatever illusionary act has been committed by me—
knowing that all this is your own work, please forgive me.
Having recited thus,
the Goddess dissolves the hosts of obstructing deities into her own body; then, with the *saṃhāramudrā*, she takes a single *nirmālya* (offering remnant) from the Goddess.
Oṃ! O Goddess dwelling on the northern peak upon the earth, born from the source of Brahmā, go, O Goddess, within me.
Having recited this and smelled that flower, one should bring the Goddess into one's own heart through the path of the breath.

Having fashioned a triangular maṇḍala in the northeast and placed that flower there, one should worship Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālinī with the remains of the Goddess’s offerings, such as the *nirmālya* and *naivedya*. Her meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
For example:
seated upon a corpse, clad in red garments and ornaments,
adorned with jewel-encrusted jewelry and decorated with a necklace of gunja berries.
A sixteen-year-old young woman with full and elevated breasts,
holding a skull-cup and a chisel in her hands, whose essential nature is the supreme light.

The best of mantra-knowers should meditate on the left and right eyes. Having thus meditated, he should worship with [the offerings] beginning with "This is the water for the feet (pādya), hrīṃ, obeisance to Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī," and ending with betel (tāmbūla). Then he should offer the bali-oblation to the Goddess with the Ucchiṣṭa-bali. Of her—

The special mantra is as follows: *ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālini sumukhi devi mahāpiśācini hrīṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*. Then, having recited the root mantra: *śrīmaddakṣiṇakālike pūjitāsi kṣamasva svāhā*. Having thus bid farewell to the Goddess, one should receive the nectar from her feet with this mantra.
In the Gaṅgā, Puṣkara, and Narmadā; in the Yamunā, Godāvarī, and Gomatī;
at the holy sites of Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, Badarī, Vārāṇasī, and the Sindhu rivers.
Within the interior of the vessel of the universe, from the Revā, Setu, Sarasvatī, and other sacred sites,
the water that has washed the feet of the Śrīcakra bestows the fruit of ten million billion ritual baths in holy fords.

Then one should place the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering) upon the head. One should apply the paste from the *yantra* as a *tilaka* on the forehead. Having given the *naivedya* (food offering) to the devotees, one should partake of it oneself. After clearing the place of worship and drawing the seed-syllable *Hūṃ* there, one should take the clay from that spot with the little finger of the left hand.
Whomever I touch or behold with my eyes,
let that very person fall into servitude, even if he were equal to Śakra himself.

With this mantra, one should apply a tilaka on the forehead. One should place the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) and other items at the root of a bilva tree or in water, or in any pure place whatsoever. Having contemplated "I am He" (so'ham), and being intent upon the conduct of a Vaiṣṇava, one should go about as one pleases.
[Thus ends the ritual manual for the worship of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā.
Oṃ tatsat. Salutations to the Guru. May it be auspicious!
